links.targetTitle: LayerZero bridge destinations are a governance-configured al

title: The LayerZero bridge's minimum delivered amount is set from the OFT's own quote immediately before sending, leaving no shortfall tolerance
content:
A.6.1.1.2.2.6.1.2.2.1.2.1.2.13.1.5 completes a procedure that looks unguarded when read one step earlier. The `SendParam` struct is built in A...13.1.4 with `minAmountLD` initialised to `0`, but that value never reaches the wire:

```
( ,, OFTReceipt memory receipt ) = ILayerZero(oftAddress).quoteOFT(sendParams);
sendParams.minAmountLD = receipt.amountReceivedLD;
```

The bound is therefore not a governance parameter and not a caller argument — it is the counterparty's **own prediction of what it will deliver**, captured in the same transaction and then held to. Setting `minAmountLD` equal to the quote rather than to the quote minus a tolerance means there is zero slack: if the actual credit falls even marginally below the quoted `amountReceivedLD`, the send reverts.

That is a defensible choice for OFT transfers specifically, because the gap between quote and delivery is deterministic (decimal-precision dust removal and configured fees), not market-driven. Contrast the Pendle path, where A...11.1.3 deliberately subtracts a rounding buffer of `5` from the router-facing minimum precisely because the arithmetic there can truncate.

The general form of the technique is worth naming: rather than trusting a counterparty or trying to model it, ask it to commit to a number and then enforce that number in the same call. It converts an unverifiable external process into a self-imposed constraint.
description: quoteOFT returns amountReceivedLD and that exact value becomes sendParams.minAmountLD, so the zero in the struct literal is a placeholder and any delivery below the quote reverts.
